propositions.text: The appellant, a Chinese citizen, appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection.
propositions.quote: XXXXXXX a citizen of China, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection.

propositions.text: The appellant has not submitted new evidence in support of her appeal.
propositions.quote: She has not submitted new evidence in support of her appeal.

propositions.text: The appellant asks the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and find her a Convention refugee or refer her claim back for re-determination.
propositions.quote: The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and find her a Convention refugee, or, in the alternative, refer her claim back to the RPD for re-determination.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant appeals the RPD decision without new evidence; the appellant asks RAD to set aside or refer back the claim.

propositions.text: Pursuant to IRPA s.111(1)(a), the RAD confirms the RPD determination and dismisses the appeal.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeal under IRPA s.111(1)(a).

propositions.text: The appellant alleged before the RPD she is a Falun Gong practitioner and described her practice and flight from China.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleged before the RPD that she is a Falun Gong practitioner. She alleges that after telling a friend that she was experiencing stress from her schooling, the friend recommended that she practice Falun Gong. She began practicing with the friend and joined her practice group as well. The group practice was subsequently raided and she went into hiding at the home of another friend. The Appellant recognized it was unsafe to remain in China and sought the assistance of a smuggler to leave the country. She travelled to the United States en route to Canada. While attempting to enter Canada illegally, she was apprehended by Canadian officials. The Appellant claims authorities in China are seeking to arrest her for her practice of Falun Gong. This led to her making a refugee claim in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant alleged to the RPD she practiced Falun Gong, fled China, and was apprehended entering Canada illegally.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the claim, finding the appellant not credible and not a Falun Gong practitioner.
propositions.quote: In a decision on December 19, 2014, the RPD rejected the claim finding that the Appellant was not a credible witness and she was not a Falun Gong practitioner.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the appellant not credible and rejected her Falun Gong claim.

propositions.text: The appellant argues the RPD erred in credibility findings on her ability to leave China, assessment of documents, and sur place claim.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its credibility findings on the following three issues: a) Her ability to leave China using her own passport b) An unreasonable assessment of her supporting documents and c) An unreasonable assessment of the Appellant's sur place claim.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD erred in credibility findings on passport use, document assessment, and sur place claim.

propositions.text: Counsel made submissions on RAD's role reviewing RPD decisions.
propositions.quote: Counsel has made submissions in regard to the role that the RAD plays in the review of an RPD decision.

propositions.text: The Federal Court in Huruglica guides that RAD conducts a hybrid appeal with independent assessment, substituting its own decision if differing from RPD.
propositions.quote: Justice Phelan states in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision.

propositions.text: RAD can respect RPD credibility findings but is not restricted to intervening only on overriding and palpable errors.
propositions.quote: [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error."

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RAD's hybrid appeal role per Huruglica, allowing independent assessment and respect for RPD credibility findings.

propositions.text: RAD will independently assess the RPD decision and afford deference to RPD credibility findings where appropriate.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Deference will be afforded to the credibility findings of the RPD or to other findings where the RPD has a particular advantage in reaching its conclusions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD will independently assess the RPD decision, deferring to RPD credibility findings as appropriate.

propositions.text: The RPD found the claimant did not credibly practice Falun Gong in China, was not wanted by authorities, was not genuine in Canada, and lacked evidence of Chinese attention.
propositions.quote: The RPD in its Reasons found: i. The claimant did not provide credible and trustworthy evidence of practicing Falun Gong in China. ii. The claimant was not wanted by the authorities in China for the practice of Falun Gong. iii. The claimant was not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in Canada and came to Canada in order to advance a fraudulent refugee claim. iv. There is insufficient evidence that the claimant's actions in Canada have come to the attention of Chinese authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the claimant not credible as a Falun Gong practitioner and lacking evidence of Chinese authorities' interest.

propositions.text: The appellant does not dispute the RPD's findings on Falun Gong practice in China.
propositions.quote: A review of the Appellant's Memorandum4 by the RAD notes the Appellant does not dispute the findings of the RPD in respect of the claimant's Falun Gong practice in China.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the appellant does not dispute RPD's findings on Falun Gong practice in China.

propositions.text: The RPD found the appellant's ability to leave China with her own passport was not credible without smuggler details.
propositions.quote: The RPD drew an adverse credibility finding based on the Appellant's ability to leave China using her own passport. The RPD noted that despite documentary evidence that security services are successful in preventing persons who are wanted from leaving the country and considering that her passport was issued after she was already wanted by the PSB due to her involvement in Falun Gong, the Appellant was still able to leave China. The RPD concluded that the use of a smuggler without details of how a smuggler was able to circumvent the vast security capabilities, was insufficient to explain the claimant's ability to secure a passport and leave without a problem.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the appellant's explanation for leaving China with her passport not credible due to lack of smuggler details.

propositions.text: The appellant submits there is no certainty whether the database exists.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the evidence before the RPD makes it clear that there is no certainty with respect to whether the database exists.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues there is no certainty the database exists.

propositions.text: The appellant relies on NDP item 10.3 stating the Ministry selected a technology company only in 2009.
propositions.quote: The Appellant relies on item 10.3 listed in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for China that states: "it was not until February 11, 2009 that the Chinese Ministry of Public Security even selected a technology company - China Information Security Technology - to deliver the system."

paragraphs.summary: The appellant relies on NDP stating the Ministry selected a technology company only in 2009.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the appellant misapprehended the evidence she relies on regarding the date of technology company selection.
propositions.quote: Although the Appellant alleges the RPD misapprehended the evidence, the RAD finds that it is the Appellant who has misapprehended the evidence she relies on.

propositions.text: The document states the article is dated Feb 11, 2009 but does not state when the company was selected.
propositions.quote: A careful reading of the document relied upon reveals that the document does not state that the PSB selected the technology company on February 11, 2009. Rather, the document refers to an article dated February 11, 2009 in which it is stated that a technology company was selected, but it does not provide a date of when that selection was made.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant misapprehended evidence; the document's article is dated 2009 but does not state when selection occurred.

propositions.text: The appellant quotes the document stating provincial cities would integrate the system in three years before nationwide implementation.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also quotes the same document as stating that the "a number of provincial level cities and municipalities would have standardized and integrated elements of this technology system in three years, after which these systems will be implemented nationwide."

paragraphs.summary: The appellant quotes the document about phased provincial then nationwide system implementation.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the appellant took the statement out of context and failed to acknowledge it refers to phase two of implementation.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant has taken this statement out of context. The Appellant fails to acknowledge that the paragraph quoted is referring to the second phase of the implementation of the system.

propositions.text: The article is dated 2009 but does not indicate when the system was implemented.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also fails to acknowledge that the article providing this information was dated in 2009; however, there is no indication in the article when the system was implemented.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant took the statement out of context and the article does not indicate when implementation occurred.

propositions.text: The article states the national PGIS initiative is phase two of Golden Shield, aiming to integrate systems nationwide in three years.
propositions.quote: ...this national PGIS initiative is part of phase two of the Golden Shield project and aims to "establish an integrated platform connecting all variations of PGIS systems throughout the country" in order to share information across various public service departments and police divisions (Ibid.). It is estimated that 100 provincial-level cities and municipalities will have standardized and integrated PGIS systems in three years, after which these systems will be implemented nationwide (Ibid.).

paragraphs.summary: The article states the PGIS initiative is phase two of Golden Shield aiming for nationwide integration in three years.

propositions.text: The same document shows the Golden Shield project was operational as early as 2003.
propositions.quote: In fact, the same document relied upon by the Appellant provides evidence that the Golden Shield project was operational as early as 2003.

paragraphs.summary: The document shows Golden Shield was operational as early as 2003.

propositions.text: The appellant refers to Wei case where the court criticized reliance on Golden Shield documentary evidence as only showing intent to implement.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also refers to Wei9 to support her argument. In that case, the reviewing court took exception to the panel's reliance on the documentary evidence related to the Golden Shield project. In particular, the court stated: "The information does not confirm that a centralised information sharing system was in place; rather it discusses the intention to put such a network in place."

paragraphs.summary: The appellant cites Wei where the court criticized reliance on Golden Shield evidence as showing intent only.

propositions.text: The RAD notes Wei was based on 2010 evidence, but the RPD relies on current documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: However, the RAD notes that the decision in Wei11 was based on the documentary evidence that existed in 2010. In the case at hand, the RPD relies on the documentary evidence in the record today.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Wei was based on 2010 evidence; here RPD relies on current documentary evidence.

propositions.text: The NDP states with certainty that the Golden Shield project is operational.
propositions.quote: Again, the RAD notes that the same National Documentation Package relied upon by the Appellant also states with certainty that the Golden Shield project is operational.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the NDP states the Golden Shield project is operational.

propositions.text: A researcher with 15 years' experience states Chinese police have nationwide computer information sharing networks.
propositions.quote: China's Public Security Departments absolutely do have nationwide computer information sharing networks, and have been working hard to develop and expand those for at least a decade....

propositions.text: Complaints exist about provincial police departments not sharing information with each other.
propositions.quote: One does read complaints about provincial police departments not being willing to share information with each other, however.

propositions.text: Information about nationwide arrest warrants is openly available on Ministry of Public Security and provincial police websites.
propositions.quote: For Chinese readers, a good deal of information about nationwide arrest warrants is openly available on the webpage of the Ministry of Public Security (www.mps.gov.cn) and on the webpages of the various provincial public security departments.

propositions.text: There has been an explosion of online police information in the past 6-7 years.
propositions.quote: There has really been an explosion of this online police information in the past 6-7 years.

paragraphs.summary: A researcher states Chinese police have nationwide computer networks, some provincial sharing issues, and much online police information available.

propositions.text: UK Operational Guidance Note states Chinese police have access to Golden Shield Project national computer database.
propositions.quote: The Chinese police have access to a National Computer Database, known as Golden Shield Project.

propositions.text: Golden Shield holds various population, criminal, and police information accessible to most police departments at county level and above.
propositions.quote: It holds information on population information, criminal records information, information on criminal fugitives, information on stolen vehicles, information on passports and exit/entry data, information on registered cars and drivers, information on police officers and information on key fire-prevention units.

propositions.text: Most police departments at county level and above and most grass-roots units can connect to Golden Shield; some remote small departments cannot yet connect.
propositions.quote: All police departments at county level and above (i.e. police departments at provincial, city and county levels) and most grass-roots units (police units below county level) can now connect to this system. There are some small police departments in remote areas that cannot yet connect to Golden Shield.

paragraphs.summary: UK guidance notes Chinese police access Golden Shield database with extensive info accessible to most police departments.

propositions.text: It is clear that such a system is in place.
propositions.quote: Based on the foregoing, it is clear that such a system is in place.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concludes a nationwide police information system is in place in China.

propositions.text: The Appellant does not address the RPD's issue about plausibility of obtaining a genuine Chinese passport after being sought by PSB.
propositions.quote: the Appellant does not address the issue raised by the RPD in respect of the plausibility of a genuine Chinese passport being issued to her following the time she alleges the PSB began to search for her on xxx, 2014.

propositions.text: Appellant testified passport was arranged by 'snakehead' but was unsure how it was arranged.
propositions.quote: Her response was, "It was arranged by the snakehead". The Appellant was further asked how this was arranged and she answered, "I'm not sure".

propositions.text: RPD concluded use of smuggler without details insufficient to explain obtaining passport and leaving China safely if sought by authorities.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded, having considered both the documentary evidence as well as the Appellant's testimony, the mere use of a smuggler without any details of how the smuggler acted to circumvent the vast security network is insufficient to explain the Appellant's ability to obtain a passport and leave China safely if the authorities were seeking her.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the Appellant did not address RPD's concern about plausibility of obtaining passport via smuggler while sought by authorities.

propositions.text: RAD reviewed documentary evidence on issuing Chinese Biometric Passports including fingerprint and signature collection.
propositions.quote: The RAD in addition reviewed the documentary evidence in respect of the issuing of Chinese Biometric Passports which states: ... the procedures of collecting the applicant's finger prints and the applicant signing [his or her] name on site are added.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD reviewed documentary evidence on biometric passport issuance requiring fingerprints and signature collection.

propositions.text: It is reasonable to expect Appellant to provide testimony confirming she supplied fingerprints and signature to smuggler to obtain passport.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that the Appellant would provide some supporting testimony to confirm that in the very least she supplied these items to the smuggler to obtain the passport.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence states passports issued by entry-exit control department of public security organ at or above county level where residence is registered.
propositions.quote: the documentary evidence states that passports are issued by the entry-exit control department of the public security organ under the people's government at or above the county level where his residence is registered.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD expects Appellant to confirm supplying biometric data to smuggler; passports issued by public security at county level or above.

propositions.text: RAD finds evidence supports RPD conclusion Appellant could not obtain passport and leave China while sought by authorities.
propositions.quote: The RAD having assessed and considered the evidence in this issue, finds this information buttresses the RPD conclusion that the Appellant would be unable to obtain a passport and leave China while being sought by the authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds evidence supports RPD's conclusion that Appellant could not obtain passport and leave China while sought.

propositions.text: RPD entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibilities, common sense, and rationality; may reject inconsistent evidence.
propositions.quote: The RPD is entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibilities, common sense and rationality, and it may reject evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole.

propositions.text: Where RPD finds lack of credibility based on plausibility inferences, there must be evidential basis for such inferences.
propositions.quote: Where the RPD finds a lack of credibility based on inferences concerning the plausibility of evidence, there must be a basis in the evidence to support such inferences.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court states RPD may reject evidence based on implausibility if supported by evidence.

propositions.text: There is evidential foundation for RPD's findings; RAD independently finds evidence supports RPD's finding on this issue.
propositions.quote: In this case, there is an evidential foundation for the RPD's findings. In having independently reviewed the evidence, the RAD finds that it supports the RPD's finding on this issue.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds evidential foundation supports RPD's findings on passport issue.

propositions.text: Appellant has not tendered persuasive evidence that PSB or other Chinese authority is pursuing her.
propositions.quote: The RAD also notes that the Appellant has not tendered any persuasive evidence that the PSB or any other authority in China is pursuing her.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, Appellant's allegations of Falun Gong practice, raid, and pursuit by PSB are not credible.
propositions.quote: the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's allegations that she was a Falun Gong practitioner in China, that her Falun Gong group was raided and that she is being pursued by the PSB is not credible.

propositions.text: RPD engaged in unreasonable analysis regarding Appellant's supporting documents.
propositions.quote: The RPD engaged in unreasonable analysis with respect to the Appellant's supporting documents

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no persuasive evidence of pursuit and finds Appellant's allegations not credible; RPD's document analysis unreasonable.

propositions.text: Appellant submits RPD erred by misconstruing evidence assessing letter supporting her Falun Gong practice in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD erred when it misconstrued the evidence in its assessment of a letter submitted in support of her practice of Falun Gong in Canada.

propositions.text: Appellant alleges RPD dismissed letter partly because her sister did not testify in support of her claim.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges the RPD dismissed the document partially on the basis that the Appellant's sister did not testify in support of her claim.

propositions.text: Appellant argues RPD concluded letter was not reflective of her Falun Gong practice because author was a fellow refugee claimant.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the panel came to the conclusion that the letter was not a reflection of the Appellant's Falun Gong practice in Canada because the author of the letter was a fellow refugee claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues RPD erred by dismissing letter supporting her Falun Gong practice due to sister's non-testimony and author's status.

propositions.text: RAD is not persuaded by Appellant's argument about RPD rejecting letter due to sister's non-testimony; argument taken out of context.
propositions.quote: The RAD in reviewing the record, finds that the Appellant's argument in respect of the RPD having rejected the letter based on the claimant's sister not testifying in support of her claim is taken out of context.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD rejects Appellant's argument that RPD dismissed letter due to sister's non-testimony as taken out of context.

propositions.text: RPD found credibility concerns with Appellant's sister, a previous refugee claimant on Falun Gong basis.
propositions.quote: The RPD roots its findings in a number of credibility concerns outlined in its reasons. The RPD went into extensive detail in describing credibility findings in respect of the Appellant's sister - a previous refugee claimant whose claim was allegedly also submitted on the basis of having been a Falun Gong practitioner.

propositions.text: RPD found contradiction in Appellant using a stranger to attest to her Falun Gong identity rather than her sister.
propositions.quote: The RPD found further contradiction in the Appellant's actions of utilizing a stranger whom she testified that she knows little about to attest to her identity as a Falun Gong practitioner in the form of a letter rather than her sister.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found credibility concerns with Appellant's sister and contradiction in using a stranger to attest to her Falun Gong identity.

propositions.text: RAD notes Appellant's testimony about letter's author was vague and lacked specificity.
propositions.quote: The RAD in reviewing the audio recording of the hearing noted that the Appellant's testimony in reference to the individual who authored the letter seemed vague and lacked specificity.

propositions.text: Appellant's testimony about letter content was hesitant, vague, and lacking specificity, undermining credibility and document's credibility.
propositions.quote: Her testimony in this regard was also hesitant, vague and lacking in specificity. The RAD finds the Appellant's ambiguous testimony further undermines the claimant's credibility as well as her identity as a Falun Gong practitioner and undermines the credibility of the document.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant's vague testimony about letter and its content undermines her and the document's credibility.

propositions.text: Letter dated October 4, 2014 states author met Appellant on September 13, 2014, knowing her for three weeks.
propositions.quote: The RAD in evaluating the document notes the letter is dated October 4, 2014 and states that the author met the Appellant on September 13, 2014, indicating that the author of the document has known the Appellant for three weeks.

propositions.text: Letter indicates they perform Falun Gong exercises together; founder states exercises alone do not define genuine practitioner.
propositions.quote: the individuals perform the five exercises associated with Falun Gong together. Master Li, the founder of Falun Gong in the text Zhuan Falun explains the performance of the exercises alone without regard for the philosophy of Falun Gong does not define that individual as a genuine Falun Gong practitioner.

propositions.text: Letter's author states Appellant is a true Falun Gong practitioner but no evidence author has expertise to judge genuineness; little weight given.
propositions.quote: the author of the letter states, "Ms. xxxx is a true Falun Gong practitioner". The RAD finds there was no evidence adduced in the record to indicate that the author of this letter has the expertise to make such a judgment and as such, little weight can be afforded to his assessment of the genuineness of the Appellant's alleged practice.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds letter's author known Appellant three weeks, letter lacks expert basis to confirm genuine Falun Gong practice, so little weight given.

propositions.text: List of Falun Gong Co-practitioners dated July 11, 2014 predates Appellant's first entry to Canada on August 30, 2014.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the document is dated July 11, 2014. Examination of the Basis of Claim (BOC) document confirms the Appellant did not enter Canada for the first time until August 30, 2014; well over one month after her alleged co-practitioners attested to her practice of Falun Gong.

propositions.text: Date contradiction undermines document authenticity; letter's author appears on list despite Appellant not yet in Canada, undermining letter's credibility.
propositions.quote: This significant contradiction in dates undermines the authenticity of the document and as such, the RAD assigns it little evidentiary weight. The RAD also notes that the author of the letter submitted in support of the Appellant's practice of Falun Gong appears on this document. Given that the author of the letter included his name on a document attesting to the fact that he was a co-practitioner of the Appellant at a time when the Appellant was not yet in Canada, the RAD finds that the credibility of the letter is also undermined.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds date contradictions undermine co-practitioner list and letter's credibility, assigning little evidentiary weight.

propositions.text: Appellant submits RPD's Falun Gong practice finding was speculative and unclear.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also submits that the RPD finding with regard to her practice of Falun Gong was speculative.

propositions.text: RAD finds Appellant's argument has some merit; RPD's analysis unclear and speculative.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant's argument has some merit. The RAD's review of the RPD's decision finds its analysis is not well articulated and its statements are unclear, leading the RPD to draw what at best can be described as a speculative conclusion.

propositions.text: RPD erroneously found letter was part of organized effort to advance fraudulent refugee claims; no basis in record for this conclusion.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the RPD erroneously found that the letter of support was part of an organized effort to support the advancement of fraudulent refugee claims. The RAD finds there is no basis in the record for the RPD to come to this conclusion.

propositions.text: RPD's implication of organized conspiracy is unfortunate but documents still warrant little weight.
propositions.quote: It is unfortunate that the RPD has implied that there is an organized conspiracy to advance fraudulent claims however there remains sufficient reason to place little weight on the documents in question.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds RPD's Falun Gong analysis speculative and erroneous about conspiracy, but documents still warrant little weight.

propositions.text: RAD concludes documents are not genuine and submission undermines Appellant's credibility and genuineness as Falun Gong practitioner.
propositions.quote: The RAD concludes after its own review and assessment of the evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, these documents are not genuine documents. The RAD finds that the submission of these non-genuine documents undermines the Appellant's credibility and further undermines the genuineness as a Falun Gong practitioner in China and in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concludes documents are not genuine and undermine Appellant's credibility and genuineness as Falun Gong practitioner.

propositions.text: Appellant submits RPD's sur place analysis is erroneous for failing to explain why her Falun Gong group would not be watched by Chinese authorities.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD's sur place analysis is erroneous because it fails to explain why the applicant's Falun Gong practice group would not be watched by the Chinese authorities.

propositions.text: Appellant quotes RPD's statement about insufficient evidence that her limited actions in Canada have come to Chinese authorities' attention.
propositions.quote: The Appellant quotes the below-noted extract from the RPD's reasons: The panel has insufficient evidence to suggest the claimant's limited actions in Canada, likely done to advance her refugee claim, have come to the attention of Chinese authorities and so would cause her any problems upon her return.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues RPD's sur place analysis erred by not explaining why her Falun Gong group would not be watched by Chinese authorities.

propositions.text: Appellant argues even if not genuine practitioner, she could be at risk if Chinese authorities learn of her Falun Gong activities in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that, even if the Appellant was not a genuine practitioner of Falun Gong, she could still be at risk if her Falun Gong activities in Canada came to the attention of Chinese authorities.

propositions.text: Appellant argues RPD failed to consider reasonable chance or serious possibility of persecution given public practice and Chinese monitoring.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to consider whether there is a reasonable chance or serious possibility of persecution of the Appellant given her public practice of Falun Gong and the documented monitoring that takes place by the Chinese government.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues RPD failed to consider risk of persecution from Chinese monitoring of her public Falun Gong practice in Canada.

propositions.text: The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument that the RPD failed to consider risk from Falun Gong activities in Canada.
propositions.quote: The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument in this regard.

propositions.text: The RPD considered risk if Chinese authorities learned of Appellant's Falun Gong activities in Canada.
propositions.quote: the RPD did consider the risk to the Appellant if the Chinese authorities became aware of her Falun Gong activities in Canada.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant was not a Falun Gong practitioner in China and that claim was made to further a fraudulent refugee claim.
propositions.quote: Having previously found the Appellant's testimony with regard to her Falun Gong affiliation in China not credible, the RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that her claim that she was a Falun Gong practitioner in China was made to further a fraudulent refugee claim.

propositions.text: The RAD conducted a full review and supports the RPD's finding that the claim was fraudulent.
propositions.quote: The RAD having conducted a full review and assessment of the record arrives at the same conclusion and supports the finding of the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the RPD considered risk from Falun Gong activities and supports RPD's finding that the Appellant's claim was fraudulent.

propositions.text: The RAD finds no persuasive evidence that Chinese authorities know of Appellant's Falun Gong practice in Canada or perceive her as genuine.
propositions.quote: there was no persuasive evidence adduced at the hearing or in her BoC form that the Appellant's practice of Falun Gong in Canada has come to the attention of Chinese authorities or that she would be perceived to be a genuine practitioner.

propositions.text: Wang decision holds sur place claim requires evidence that refugee claim came to attention of origin country authorities.
propositions.quote: the Federal Court Trial Division decision in Wang, which held that a sur place claim could not be maintained in the absence of evidence that the making of the refugee claim had specifically come to the attention of the authorities of the claimant's country of origin.

propositions.text: The Appellant does not argue that the RPD misconstrued the facts in Wang.
propositions.quote: The Appellant does not submit that the RPD has misconstrued the facts in Wang.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no evidence Chinese authorities know of Appellant's Falun Gong practice; Wang requires such evidence; Appellant does not dispute RPD's application of Wang.

propositions.text: The RAD finds on balance of probabilities that Appellant joined Falun Gong group in Canada to support a fraudulent refugee claim.
propositions.quote: the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of the findings noted above, that the Appellant joined a Falun Gong group in Canada only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges her desire to practice Falun Gong arose from circumstances in China and continued practice in Canada is based on adherence to China practice.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has alleged that her desire to initiate the practice of Falun Gong took place as a result of circumstances which occurred in China. She alleges her continued practice of her alleged belief system in Canada is based on her adherence to her practice in China.

propositions.text: The RAD found no evidence of conversion in Canada and that Appellant was not a Falun Gong practitioner in China.
propositions.quote: Having found that she was not a Falun Gong practitioner in China and having no evidence of conversion in Canada

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant joined Falun Gong group in Canada to support a fraudulent claim; Appellant alleges practice began in China but RAD found no evidence of that.

propositions.text: The RAD finds Appellant is not a genuine Falun Gong adherent nor perceived as one in China.
propositions.quote: the RAD finds that the Appellant is not a genuine adherent of Falun Gong, nor would she be perceived to be one in China.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant is not a genuine Falun Gong adherent nor perceived as such in China.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges the RPD erred in rejecting her claim.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has alleged that the RPD erred in rejecting her claim.

propositions.text: The RPD made an error in drawing a speculative conclusion but overall adverse credibility findings justify confirming RPD's determination.
propositions.quote: Notwithstanding the error made by the RPD in drawing a speculative conclusion, the RAD finds after its review and assessment of all of the evidence in the record, that the cumulative adverse credibility findings and significant uncontested credibility findings of the RPD are sufficient for the RAD to confirm the RPD's overall determination.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges RPD erred; RAD finds despite one error, RPD's adverse credibility findings justify confirming its decision.

propositions.text: The Appellant has not met burden to show serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment or torture in China.
propositions.quote: the Appellant has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility that she would be persecuted or that she would be personally subjected to a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in China.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant failed to prove serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment or torture in China.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed.
